bib.title: Chapter 11. Improvement Loops (Building Applications with AI Agents)
bib.venue: book chapter (O'Reilly, per source folder name; not printed in the PDF text)

question: How can an agent system be built to learn from its failures and improve continuously, through feedback pipelines, experimentation and continuous learning?
contributions: Frames continuous improvement as three linked parts: feedback pipelines, experimentation frameworks, continuous learning.
Walks a Security Operations Center (SOC) analyst agent built with LangGraph through each part, with DSPy code for prompt and tool refinement.

limits: No experiments, benchmarks or measured gains; all numbers are illustrative thresholds or hypothetical examples.
Code examples use mock tools, a handful of synthetic examples and exact-match metrics, which the chapter says to replace in production.

The chapter's own limitations table: feedback pipelines depend on data quality and may miss novel issues; experimentation needs ample data and is resource-heavy; continuous learning risks overfitting or regression and is costly.
In-context adaptations are ephemeral and lost when the session ends.
Shadow deployments cannot exercise HITL-dependent agents without exposure risk; A/B tests are harder with long-term state.
Bayesian bandits need rewards that reflect true goals and can create pathological feedback loops.

The concluding summary says continuous learning focuses on in-context learning, though offline retraining is also covered. Online learning is announced as a core mechanism but has no section of its own.
Tools and model names (GPT-5, gpt-4o-mini, DSPy API calls) may date.
practices: Cluster similar failures from logs and traces automatically and flag high-impact ones, rather than having engineers comb raw logs (Feedback Pipelines).
Run RCA in four steps: workflow tracing, fault localization, pattern recognition, impact assessment (Automated Issue Detection and RCA).
Escalate to humans by least model certainty or most consequential outcome, combining uncertainty with consequence into a risk score (HITL Review).
Log decisions and rationales from human review so incidents are reproducible and organisational learning accumulates (HITL Review).
Refine prompts by rewriting for clarity, adding positive and negative exemplars, decomposing tasks and expanding context (Prompt Refinement).
Use DSPy optimisers (MIPROv2, BootstrapFewshot) with a metric and 100+ annotated examples to refine prompts and tool-selection (Prompt and Tool Refinement).
Document each refinement with the problem observed, the change made and how effectiveness will be measured (Prompt and Tool Refinement).
Validate refinements offline on held-out logs or synthetic cases, then via shadow deployments or A/B tests, and monitor after deployment (Prompt and Tool Refinement).

Aggregate feedback into one backlog with deduplication, tagging and links to context; prioritise by frequency, severity, feasibility, strategic alignment and recurrence/risk (Aggregating and Prioritizing).
Roll out through staging, shadow, canary, rolling or blue/green deployment (Experimentation).

For A/B tests: clear metrics, sufficient sample size, prevent cross-contamination, monitor short- and long-term effects, use sticky assignment or session-level tests when state persists (A/B Testing).
For bandits: use neutral priors and regularisation, reward true goals, watch for pathological feedback loops (Bayesian Bandits).
Promote successful in-context fixes into prompt engineering, workflow updates or retraining (In-Context Learning).
Offline retraining: curate labelled production traces, update via few-shot optimisation or fine-tuning (e.g., LoRA), validate offline then in shadow before rollout (Offline Retraining).
